record.original_question: Must every infinite-dimensional F-space that is not locally bounded contain an infinite-dimensional nuclear subspace?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM 11. - Does each non-locally bounded infinite dimensional F-space contain an infinite dimensional nuclear space ?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An F-space is a topological vector space over the real or complex field whose topology is induced by a complete translation-invariant metric. An F-space X is called locally bounded if there exists a neighborhood U of 0 that is bounded (i.e., for every neighborhood V of 0 there exists t>0 with U ⊆ tV); equivalently, its topology is given by a p-homogeneous F-norm for some 0<p≤1. A topological vector space N is called nuclear if its topology can be defined by a family of seminorms {p_α} such that for every α there exists β with p_α ≤ p_β and the canonical map of the local Banach space associated to p_β into that associated to p_α is a nuclear (trace-class) operator.

Question: Does every infinite-dimensional F-space that is not locally bounded contain an infinite-dimensional nuclear subspace?
